title: Philemon
hook: a short note asking a slave owner to receive Onesimus as a beloved brother
carry: no longer a servant, but a brother

segments.voice: Yesterday, epistle: Paul's letters as real mail, with a scribe's hello and a list of friends.

Ever written a note on someone else's behalf? A reference, or a text to smooth things over between friends: you choose every word; someone's future rides on it. Paul's letter to Philemon is that. It's one page, written from prison to Philemon, a believer with a church meeting in his home. It's about Onesimus, who is enslaved in Philemon's household, and has left. Somehow he found Paul in prison and became a believer. Now Paul sends him back carrying this letter. Philemon has the law on his side, and the power to punish. Everything depends on this page.
screen: `A NOTE FOR SOMEONE ELSE.` → `ONE PAGE, FROM PRISON.` → `ONESIMUS GOES BACK.`

segments.voice: Watch how Paul does it. He could order Philemon to do the right thing, but would rather appeal, for love's sake. He calls Onesimus my son, my very heart. He even jokes, since Onesimus means useful: "Which in time past was to thee unprofitable, but now profitable to thee and to me." Then the real request. Take him back, the King James Bible says, "Not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved." The Greek word translated servant is doulos: slave. Paul asks a slave owner to receive an enslaved man as a brother, in the flesh and in the Lord. Then he signs a blank check: "If he hath wronged thee, or oweth thee ought, put that on mine account." I, Paul, write this with my own hand: I will repay it. Near the end: knowing you'll do even more than I say. Now the honest part. The letter never says, in so many words, set him free. We don't know why Onesimus left, or what Philemon did next. The Bible is silent. Over the centuries, some Christians used Paul's letters to defend slavery, and others, including many who fought to end it, read this page as pointing the other way: once a man is your brother, how can he be your property? Later, a letter by Ignatius of Antioch names a bishop of Ephesus called Onesimus. Some wonder if it's the same man. Nobody knows. What's left is one page, where Paul puts his name on the line for someone with less power, and asks for a new word: brother.
screen: `FOR LOVE'S SAKE, NOT ORDERS.` · `ONESIMUS MEANS USEFUL.` · `PUT THAT ON MINE ACCOUNT.` · `THE BIBLE IS SILENT ON WHAT CAME NEXT.` · then, large: `A BROTHER BELOVED.`

segments.voice: Think of someone with less say than those around them: a new employee, a kid, someone who cleans the office after everyone leaves, someone whose English is still new. Picture putting in a word for them, as Paul did: a thank you said where the boss can hear, a good reference, something put on your account. If you pray, you can pray for them by name.
Philemon. Paul's one-page letter, asking a slave owner to receive Onesimus as a beloved brother.
Your line: no longer a servant, but a brother. Tomorrow, a letter to a quarreling church. Day eighty-eight, done.

howItsDone: Philemon is read in churches as a letter about reconciliation and about how faith changes relationships of power. It was also central in debates over slavery, when abolitionists and defenders of slavery read it in opposite ways.

fork.setup: you're Paul, in prison. Onesimus has to go back to Philemon, who has every legal right to punish him. what do you write?
options: an order: free him at once.
an appeal: receive him as a brother, and charge any debt to me.
nothing. it's between the two of them.
fork.reveal: Paul appeals for love's sake: not now as a servant, but a brother beloved. if he owes thee anything, put that on mine account.

original.note: Greek: useful, profitable. The root of Paul's pun.

trapdoor: what you thought: a short, forgettable page between longer letters.
what it means: Paul puts his own name and money on the line to ask a slave owner to receive an enslaved man as a brother.
what a scholar hears: doulos means slave, Onesimus means useful, the outcome is unknown, and the letter was read in opposite ways in the slavery debates.

notes: Why Onesimus left is debated (runaway; sent on an errand; seeking Paul as a mediator). The script says only that he 'has left' and that the letter doesn't tell us why.
History of use in slavery debates, stated briefly and without drama; confirm tone.
Ignatius's letter to the Ephesians (early 2nd century) names a bishop Onesimus; identification with Philemon's Onesimus is speculative, and the script says nobody knows.
'In the flesh, as well as in the Lord' paraphrases Philemon 1:16b ('both in the flesh, and in the Lord'). Confirm.
The index carry 'no longer a servant, but a brother' paraphrases 1:16; kept exactly as the index gives it.
